lessons.title: Hysteresis and remembered branches
lessons.expression: x³ − x − b = 0; retain the nearest stable branch
lessons.setting: A declared quasi-static branch-following rule samples 81 controls. Stable roots satisfy 3x²−1>0. A snap selects the other stable root after the followed branch disappears; no transient motion, switching rate or global minimum rule is simulated.
lessons.limits: A declared quasi-static branch-following rule samples 81 controls. Stable roots satisfy 3x²−1>0. A snap selects the other stable root after the followed branch disappears; no transient motion, switching rate or global minimum rule is simulated.
lessons.question: Why can the same dial setting hold two different positions?
lessons.context: A toy snap mechanism rests in one of two wells. Raise its control dial, then lower it again. The mechanism follows its current stable branch until that branch disappears. Returning the dial to zero can leave it in a different well. The chosen history is visible, so position is not silently inferred from the dial alone.
lessons.rule: At each whole sweep step, solve the stationary cubic. Among its stable roots choose the one nearest the preceding selected root. Start at the unique root for b=−0.6, or b=0.6 for the reversed history.
titles: Zero dial on the outward sweep

lessons.title: Gradient flow and falling potential
lessons.setting: V(x,y)=(a x²+b y²)/2, with a,b positive and a fixed start (2,1). The exact continuous solution is used; there is no time-step parameter or numerical integrator. This is a constructed controller model.
lessons.limits: V(x,y)=(a x²+b y²)/2, with a,b positive and a fixed start (2,1). The exact continuous solution is used; there is no time-step parameter or numerical integrator. This is a constructed controller model.
lessons.question: What makes a continuously corrected position lose potential?
lessons.context: An ideal camera mount starts two units horizontally and one unit vertically from alignment. Its controller continuously corrects each coordinate using the negative gradient of a quadratic cost. Change the two return rates. The point can curve toward alignment while the cost falls continuously.
lessons.latex: V(x,y)=\frac{a x^2+b y^2}{2},\quad \dot x=-ax,\quad\dot y=-by,\quad x(t)=2e^{-at},\quad y(t)=e^{-bt},\quad \frac{dV}{dt}=-\|\nabla V\|^2.
lessons.rule: Evaluate the exact exponential response of each coordinate from the fixed start (2,1), substitute it into the quadratic potential, and use the chain rule to obtain minus the squared gradient norm.
titles: Give both coordinates the same rate

lessons.title: A circle needs more than one chart
lessons.setting: The unit circle is covered by two stereographic charts. A chosen projection omits its own pole, although the circle is smooth there. Coordinate values are numerical and may leave the displayed window; a chart is not an isometric map.
lessons.limits: The unit circle is covered by two stereographic charts. A chosen projection omits its own pole, although the circle is smooth there. Coordinate values are numerical and may leave the displayed window; a chart is not an isometric map.
lessons.primaryLabel: A circle needs more than one chart
lessons.question: Can a smooth circle need a second coordinate map?
lessons.context: A marker moves around a circular track. To give its position one straight-line coordinate, project a line from a chosen pole through the marker. The coordinate grows large near that pole and is unavailable at the pole itself. Switch the projection pole: the track and marker stay in place while their coordinate changes.
lessons.rule: Compute the unit-circle point from its angle. Project from the north or south pole to the horizontal coordinate line. A chart excludes its chosen pole; the other chart covers that point.
titles: Give the rightmost point a coordinate
Cover that point with the other chart

lessons.title: Local coordinates on a sphere
lessons.setting: Two stereographic charts cover the unit sphere. The north chart excludes only the north pole, and the south chart excludes only the south pole. Longitude is not unique at a pole, but the point and the other chart remain well defined. Geometry uses a labeled fixed 3D projection, not a separate Spatial tab.
lessons.limits: Two stereographic charts cover the unit sphere. The north chart excludes only the north pole, and the south chart excludes only the south pole. Longitude is not unique at a pole, but the point and the other chart remain well defined. Geometry uses a labeled fixed 3D projection, not a separate Spatial tab.
lessons.question: How can a curved sphere have two local coordinates?
lessons.context: Place a marker on a globe and choose a projection pole. A line through that pole maps the marker to a coordinate plane. Change latitude, longitude or the projection pole. The globe point and its two plane coordinates are shown separately, so a missing coordinate at a pole is not mistaken for a defect in the globe.
lessons.rule: Locate the unit-sphere point from latitude and longitude, then apply the selected stereographic chart. The primary result is the plane-coordinate radius; it is different from the fixed sphere radius one.
titles: Turn a point above the equator
Cover the pole from the south

lessons.title: Perturbing a rule, not just a starting point
lessons.setting: This compares two explicit one-dimensional families on the line. The linear family retains one attracting equilibrium; the fold at ε=0 changes its equilibrium count under arbitrarily small signed shifts. This is a bounded introduction to structural stability, not a general certificate over all perturbations or domains.
lessons.limits: This compares two explicit one-dimensional families on the line. The linear family retains one attracting equilibrium; the fold at ε=0 changes its equilibrium count under arbitrarily small signed shifts. This is a bounded introduction to structural stability, not a general certificate over all perturbations or domains.
lessons.primaryLabel: Perturbing a rule, not just a starting point
lessons.question: What survives when the correction rule itself changes?
lessons.context: Compare two toy alignment rules. One always pulls toward a shifted target; the other is balanced at a fold. Move a small offset in the rule rather than moving the starting position. One family keeps a single attracting balance point, while the critical family can gain or lose balance points.
lessons.rule: Set each selected velocity rule equal to zero. Compare the number and local type of its equilibria with the zero-offset rule; the two explicit perturbation families illustrate different robustness.
